sentences.zh: ◎魏韋郭魏元忠，宋州宋城人。

translations.literal: ◎ Wei, Wei, and Guo — Wei Yuanzhong. Wei Yuanzhong was a man of Songcheng in Songzhou.
translations.idiomatic: Wei, Wei, and Guo — Wei Yuanzhong. Yuanzhong was a native of Songcheng in Songzhou.

sentences.zh: 為太學生，跌蕩少檢，久不調，盩厔人江融曉兵術，元忠從之遊，盡傳所學。

translations.literal: He was a student at the Imperial University, unrestrained and little restrained, long without appointment. Jiang Rong of Zhouzhi understood military arts; Yuanzhong followed him in study and received in full all he had to teach.
translations.idiomatic: While a student at the Imperial University he was free-spirited and undisciplined, and for a long time received no office. Jiang Rong of Zhouzhi was versed in military science; Yuanzhong studied under him and mastered everything his teacher knew.

sentences.zh: 儀鳳中，吐蕃數盜邊，元忠上封事洛陽宮，言命將用兵之要曰：

translations.literal: In the Yifeng era the Tibetans repeatedly raided the borders. Yuanzhong submitted a sealed memorial at the Luoyang palace, stating the essentials of appointing generals and employing troops, saying:
translations.idiomatic: During the Yifeng reign (676–679), as Tibetans repeatedly raided the frontier, Yuanzhong submitted a sealed memorial at Luoyang on the essentials of choosing commanders and waging war. He wrote:

sentences.zh: 天下之柄有二，文武而已，至制勝禦人，其道一也。

translations.literal: The handles of All-under-Heaven are two—civil and military alone; as for overcoming the enemy and controlling men, the Way is one.
translations.idiomatic: The realm rests on two powers, civil and military; yet to prevail over foes and govern men, the underlying principle is the same.

sentences.zh: 今言武者先騎射，不稽之權略；

translations.literal: Now those who speak of the military put riding and archery first and do not examine strategy.
translations.idiomatic: Today men who speak of war begin with horsemanship and archery and never weigh strategic calculation.

sentences.zh: 言文者首篇章，不取之經綸。

translations.literal: Those who speak of letters put compositions first and do not take statecraft.
translations.idiomatic: Those who speak of letters prize literary composition and ignore the art of governing the state.

sentences.zh: 臣觀魏、晉、齊、梁才固不乏，然何益治亂哉！

translations.literal: Your servant observes that Wei, Jin, Qi, and Liang indeed did not lack talent—yet what did it avail order and disorder!
translations.idiomatic: I see that Wei, Jin, Qi, and Liang were never short of talent—yet what did that avail for peace or ruin?

sentences.zh: 養由基射能穿劄，不止鄢陵之奔，陸機識能辨亡，無救河橋之敗，斷可見已。

translations.literal: Yang Youji's shooting could pierce a willow leaf, yet it did not stop the flight at Yanling; Lu Ji's discernment could recognize ruin, yet it did not save defeat at Heqiao—the conclusion is plain.
translations.idiomatic: Yang Youji could shoot through a willow leaf, yet that did not halt the rout at Yanling; Lu Ji could foresee collapse, yet could not avert disaster at Heqiao. The lesson is clear.

sentences.zh: 夫才生於世，世實須才。

translations.literal: Talent is born in an age, and the age truly needs talent.
translations.idiomatic: Talent arises in its time, and every age truly needs talent.

sentences.zh: 何世而不生才？

translations.literal: What age does not produce talent?
translations.idiomatic: What age has ever lacked men of ability?

sentences.zh: 何才而不資世？

translations.literal: What talent does not rely on the age?
translations.idiomatic: What talent does not depend on its age to flourish?

sentences.zh: 故物有不求，未有無物之歲；

translations.literal: Thus there are things not sought, yet there is no year without things.
translations.idiomatic: Some goods go unclaimed, yet no year lacks goods altogether.

sentences.zh: 士有不用，未有無士之時也。

translations.literal: There are gentlemen not employed, yet there is no time without gentlemen.
translations.idiomatic: Some men of talent go unused, yet there has never been an age without such men.

sentences.zh: 誌士在富貴與賤貧，皆思立功名以傳於後，然知己難而所遇罕。

translations.literal: Men of resolve, whether in wealth and honor or in low estate and poverty, all wish to establish merit and fame to pass to posterity—yet a true knower is hard to find and what one meets is rare.
translations.idiomatic: Men of ambition, whether rich or poor, all wish to win merit and leave a name to posterity—yet true patrons are hard to find and fair chances are few.

sentences.zh: 士之懷琬琰就煨塵、抱棟幹困溝壑者，悠悠之人直睹此士之貧賤，安知其方略哉！

translations.literal: Gentlemen who embrace jade yet approach smoldering dust, who hold pillar timber yet are trapped in gullies—the multitude of men merely see this gentleman's poverty and low station; how would they know his strategy!
translations.idiomatic: Men who carry jade in their hearts yet live in ashes, who hold timbers fit for pillars yet languish in ditches—the crowd sees only their poverty. How would the many know their true capacity?

sentences.zh: 故漢拜韓信，舉軍驚笑；

translations.literal: Thus when Han enfeoffed Han Xin, the whole army was startled and laughed.
translations.idiomatic: When Han enfeoffed Han Xin, the whole army was astonished and laughed.

sentences.zh: 蜀用魏延，群臣觖望。

translations.literal: When Shu employed Wei Yan, the ministers were discontent.
translations.idiomatic: When Shu employed Wei Yan, the ministers murmured in resentment.

sentences.zh: 此富貴者易為善，貧賤者難為功也。

translations.literal: This is why the rich and honored easily do good, while the poor and low find achievement hard.
translations.idiomatic: Thus the favored find it easy to do good, while the obscure find it hard to achieve anything.

sentences.zh: 昔漢文帝不知魏尚賢而囚之，知李廣才而不用，乃嘆其生不逢時。

translations.literal: Formerly Emperor Wen of Han did not know that Wei Shang was worthy and imprisoned him; he knew Li Guang had talent yet did not employ him, and then sighed that he was born out of season.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Wen of Han once failed to see Wei Shang's worth and imprisoned him; he knew Li Guang's talent yet would not use him, and then lamented that Li was born out of season.

sentences.zh: 夫以廣之才，天下無雙，時方歲事匈奴，而卒不任。

translations.literal: With Guang's talent, unmatched in All-under-Heaven, at a time when yearly campaigns were waged against the Xiongnu, in the end he was not entrusted.
translations.idiomatic: Li Guang's ability was unmatched in the realm, yet at the very hour when the court campaigned yearly against the Xiongnu, he was never given command.

sentences.zh: 故近不知尚、廣之賢，而遠想廉頗、李牧，馮唐是以知其有而不能用也。

translations.literal: Thus the near did not know the worth of Shang and Guang, yet longed for Lian Po and Li Mu from afar—therefore Feng Tang knew they existed yet could not be employed.
translations.idiomatic: The court did not recognize the worth of Wei Shang and Li Guang close at hand, yet yearned for Lian Po and Li Mu from ages past. Feng Tang knew such men existed yet could not put them to use.

sentences.zh: 此身為時主所知，不得盡其才也。

translations.literal: This is being known to the ruler of the age yet unable to exhaust one's talent.
translations.idiomatic: This is the case of a man known to his sovereign yet unable to give his full ability.

sentences.zh: 晉羊祜謀舉吳，賈充、荀勖沮之，祜嘆曰：「天下事不如意十常七八。」

translations.literal: In Jin, Yang Hu planned to raise forces against Wu; Jia Chong and Xun Xu obstructed him. Hu sighed and said: "Under Heaven, things go against one's wishes seven or eight times in ten.
translations.idiomatic: In Jin, Yang Hu planned an expedition against Wu, but Jia Chong and Xun Xu blocked him. Hu sighed, "Under Heaven, things go wrong seven or eight times in ten.

sentences.zh: 以二人不同，終不大舉。

translations.literal: Because the two men differed, in the end no great campaign was launched.
translations.idiomatic: Because these two men disagreed, no major campaign was ever launched.

sentences.zh: 此據立功之地，而不獲展其誌也。

translations.literal: This is holding ground where merit may be achieved yet not obtaining scope to fulfill one's aims.
translations.idiomatic: This is holding a post where merit might be won yet never gaining scope to fulfill one's aims.

sentences.zh: 布衣之人，懷奇抱策，而望朝奏夕召，豈易得哉？

translations.literal: Men in plain cloth who harbor wonders and embrace stratagems yet hope to be summoned in the morning after memorializing at dawn—are they easily obtained?
translations.idiomatic: Commoners who harbor great plans and hope for appointment the very day they submit a memorial—are such men easily found?

sentences.zh: 臣願歷訪文武五品以上，得無有智如羊祜、武如李廣而不得騁其才者乎？

translations.literal: Your servant wishes to visit in turn all civil and military officials of the fifth rank and above—might there not be some wise as Yang Hu, martial as Li Guang, yet unable to gallop forth their talent?
translations.idiomatic: I ask that Your Majesty inquire among all civil and military officials of the fifth rank and above whether any are wise as Yang Hu or martial as Li Guang yet unable to exercise their gifts.

sentences.zh: 使各言其誌，毋令久失職。

translations.literal: Have each state his aims and do not let them long lose office.
translations.idiomatic: Let each state his aims, and do not let capable men languish long without office.

sentences.zh: 又言：

translations.literal: He also stated:
translations.idiomatic: He further wrote:

sentences.zh: 人無常俗，政有治亂；

translations.literal: Men have no fixed customs; government has order and disorder.
translations.idiomatic: Human conduct has no fixed pattern; government may bring order or chaos.

sentences.zh: 軍無常勝，將有能否。

translations.literal: Armies have no constant victory; generals have ability or lack it.
translations.idiomatic: Armies do not win every battle; commanders differ in ability.

sentences.zh: 兵為王者大事，存亡系焉，將非其任，則殄人敗國。

translations.literal: Arms are the great affair of a king; survival and ruin depend on them. If the general is not equal to his charge, men are destroyed and the state defeated.
translations.idiomatic: War is the sovereign's greatest concern, on which survival depends. The wrong commander destroys armies and ruins the state.

sentences.zh: 齊段孝玄有言：「持大兵如擎盤水，一致蹉跌，求止可得哉」」周亞夫堅壁以挫吳、楚，司馬懿閉營而困諸葛亮，此皆全軍制勝，不戰而卻敵。

translations.literal: Duan Xiaoxuan of Qi said: "Holding a great army is like carrying a tray of water—one slip, and can you make it stop?" Zhou Yafu held fast in his walls to break Wu and Chu; Sima Yi closed camp to weary Zhuge Liang—all preserved the army and prevailed, repelling the foe without battle.
translations.idiomatic: Duan Xiaoxuan of Qi said, "Commanding a great army is like carrying a tray of water—one stumble and you cannot halt the spill." Zhou Yafu held his walls and broke Wu and Chu; Sima Yi shut his camps and wore down Zhuge Liang. Each preserved his army and prevailed without fighting.

sentences.zh: 是知大將臨戎，以智為本。

translations.literal: From this one knows that when a great general faces battle, wisdom is the root.
translations.idiomatic: Thus when a great commander takes the field, wisdom is the foundation.

sentences.zh: 今之用人，類將家子，或死事孤兒，進非幹略，雖竭力盡誠，不免於傾敗，若之何用之？

translations.literal: Today's employment of men is mostly sons of generals' families or orphans of those who died in service. Their advancement is not from capacity and strategy; though they exhaust strength and utmost loyalty, they cannot escape collapse—how can such men be used?
translations.idiomatic: Today appointments go mostly to sons of generals or orphans of the fallen. They lack strategic talent; though they serve with utmost loyalty, defeat is inevitable. How can such men be entrusted with command?

sentences.zh: 且建功者，言其所濟，不言所來；

translations.literal: Moreover, for those who achieve merit, one speaks of what they accomplished, not whence they came.
translations.idiomatic: For men who win merit, speak of what they achieved, not of their origins.

sentences.zh: 言其所能，不言所藉。

translations.literal: Speak of what they can do, not what they relied upon.
translations.idiomatic: Praise what they can do, not whose name they borrowed.

sentences.zh: 若陳湯、呂蒙、馬隆、孟觀悉出貧賤，而勛伐甚高，不聞其家世將帥也。

translations.literal: Chen Tang, Lü Meng, Ma Long, and Meng Guan all came from poverty and low estate, yet their achievements in merit were very high—one does not hear that their families were generations of commanders.
translations.idiomatic: Chen Tang, Lü Meng, Ma Long, and Meng Guan all rose from humble origins, yet won great merit—and none came from a line of generals.

sentences.zh: 故陰陽不和，揠士為相；

translations.literal: Thus when yin and yang are not in harmony, a commoner is pulled up to be chancellor.
translations.idiomatic: When yin and yang fall out of harmony, a commoner may be raised to chancellor.

sentences.zh: 蠻貊不廷，擢校為將。

translations.literal: When the barbarians of Man and Mo do not attend court, a clerk is promoted to general.
translations.idiomatic: When barbarians refuse to submit, a clerk may be promoted to general.

sentences.zh: 今以四海之廣，億兆之眾，豈無卓越之士？

translations.literal: Now with the breadth of the four seas and the multitude of a hundred million—are there truly no outstanding gentlemen?
translations.idiomatic: Within the four seas and among a hundred million subjects, can there truly be no outstanding men?

sentences.zh: 臣恐未之思乎！

translations.literal: Your servant fears that one has not yet thought on it!
translations.idiomatic: I fear Your Majesty has not yet looked hard enough!

sentences.zh: 又賞者禮之基，罰者刑之本。

translations.literal: Moreover, reward is the foundation of ritual; punishment is the root of penal law.
translations.idiomatic: Reward is the foundation of ritual; punishment is the root of penal law.

sentences.zh: 禮崇則謀夫竭其能，賞厚則義士輕其死，刑正故君子勖其心，罰重則小人懲其過。

translations.literal: When ritual is honored, strategists exhaust their ability; when rewards are generous, men of righteousness lightly regard death. When penal law is correct, gentlemen are encouraged in heart; when punishments are heavy, petty men are chastened for their faults.
translations.idiomatic: Honor ritual and strategists give their all; make rewards generous and loyal men lightly face death. Make law just and gentlemen steel their resolve; make punishments weighty and the base fear their faults.

sentences.zh: 賞罰者軍國之綱紀，政教之藥石。

translations.literal: Reward and punishment are the cords and nets of army and state, the medicine and stone of government and teaching.
translations.idiomatic: Reward and punishment are the sinews of army and state, the medicine of government and instruction.

sentences.zh: 吐蕃本非強敵，而薛仁貴、郭待封至棄甲喪師，脫身以免。

translations.literal: The Tibetans were originally no strong foe, yet Xue Rengui and Guo Daifeng even cast off armor and lost the army, escaping with their persons spared.
translations.idiomatic: The Tibetans were never a formidable enemy, yet Xue Rengui and Guo Daifeng abandoned their armor, lost their armies, and escaped with their lives.

sentences.zh: 國家寬政，罪止削除，網漏吞舟，何以過此。

translations.literal: The state is lenient in policy; guilt stops at removal from office. The net leaks and swallows the great boat—how can one surpass this?
translations.idiomatic: The state's lenient policy stops at demotion and dismissal. The net leaks so wide it could swallow a boat—what fault could exceed this?

sentences.zh: 雖陛下顧收後效，然朝廷所少，豈此一二人乎？

translations.literal: Although Your Majesty looks to gather later merit, yet what the court lacks—is it only these one or two men?
translations.idiomatic: Though Your Majesty hopes for future service from them, is the court so short of men that only these one or two matter?

sentences.zh: 夫賞不勸，謂之止善，罰不懲，謂之縱惡。

translations.literal: When reward does not encourage, it is called halting good; when punishment does not chasten, it is called indulging evil.
translations.idiomatic: Rewards that do not encourage are called halting virtue; punishments that do not chasten are called indulging vice.

sentences.zh: 臣誠疏賤，幹非其事，豈欲間陛下君臣生薄厚哉？

translations.literal: Your servant is truly coarse and low, meddling in what is not his affair—does he wish to set distance between Your Majesty and your ministers in thick and thin?
translations.idiomatic: I am humble and presumptuous to speak on matters not my own. Do I wish to sow discord between Your Majesty and your ministers? By no means.

sentences.zh: 正以刑賞一虧，百年不復。

translations.literal: It is precisely because once reward and punishment are impaired, a hundred years may not restore them.
translations.idiomatic: Once reward and punishment are compromised, a century may not restore them.

sentences.zh: 故國無賞罰，雖堯、舜不能為。

translations.literal: Thus a state without reward and punishment—even Yao and Shun could not govern.
translations.idiomatic: A state without reward and punishment cannot be governed even by Yao and Shun.

sentences.zh: 今罰既不行，賞復難信，故議者皆謂比日征行，虛立賞格，而無其實。

translations.literal: Now punishment is already not enforced and rewards again are hard to trust; therefore discussants all say that in recent campaigns empty reward scales were set up without substance.
translations.idiomatic: Punishment goes unenforced and rewards cannot be trusted, so critics say recent campaigns announced reward scales that were never honored.

sentences.zh: 蓋忘大體之臣恐賚勛庸，竭府庫，留意錐刀，以為益中國，所謂惜毫厘失千里者也。

translations.literal: Ministers who forget the great body fear bestowing merit and achievement, exhausting the treasury, and fix their minds on knife-points, thinking this benefits the central state—this is what is called sparing a hair's breadth and losing a thousand li.
translations.idiomatic: Ministers who lose sight of the larger picture fear rewarding merit and emptying the treasury. They count pennies, thinking to benefit the realm—yet this is to save a hair and lose a thousand li.

sentences.zh: 且黔首雖微，不可以欺，安有寓不信之令，設虛賞之格乎？

translations.literal: Moreover, though the black-headed people are slight, they cannot be deceived—how can there be orders lodged in disbelief and empty reward scales set up?
translations.idiomatic: The common people, though humble, cannot be deceived. How can the throne issue orders no one believes and promise rewards never paid?

sentences.zh: 自蘇定方平遼東，李勣破平壤，賞既不行，勛亦淹廢，歲月紛淆，真偽相錯。

translations.literal: Since Su Dingfang pacified Liaodong and Li Ji broke Pyongyang, rewards have not been carried out and merit records also lie neglected; years and months are tangled, truth and falsehood intermixed.
translations.idiomatic: Since Su Dingfang pacified Liaodong and Li Ji took Pyongyang, rewards have gone unpaid and merit rolls neglected, until years of confusion have mingled truth with falsehood.

sentences.zh: 臣以吏不奉法，慢自京師，偽勛所由，主司過也，其則不遠，近在尚書省中。

translations.literal: Your servant holds that officials do not uphold the law, arrogance beginning from the capital; false merit records arise from the fault of the responsible offices—the model is not far, close at hand within the Department of State Affairs.
translations.idiomatic: Officials do not uphold the law, and arrogance begins in the capital. False merit records stem from the fault of the responsible offices—the proof lies close at hand, within the Department of State Affairs itself.

sentences.zh: 然未聞斬一臺郎、戮一令史，使天下知之。

translations.literal: Yet one has not heard of beheading a bureau director or executing a clerk to let All-under-Heaven know.
translations.idiomatic: Yet not one bureau director has been beheaded, not one clerk executed, to make the realm take notice.

sentences.zh: 陛下何照遠而不照近哉？

translations.literal: Why does Your Majesty illuminate the distant and not the near?
translations.idiomatic: Why does Your Majesty see what is far yet overlook what is near?

sentences.zh: 神州化首，文昌政本，治亂攸在，臣故冒死而言。

translations.literal: The divine land is the head of transformation; the Literary Glory is the root of government—order and disorder depend on this; therefore your servant dares speak at risk of death.
translations.idiomatic: The realm is the source of civilization; the Department of State Affairs is the root of government. Order and chaos depend on it. That is why I speak at the risk of my life.

sentences.zh: 夫明鑒所以照形，往事所以知今，臣請借近以為諭：貞觀中，萬年尉司馬玄景舞文飾智，以邀乾沒，太宗棄之都市；

translations.literal: Bright mirrors are for illuminating forms; past affairs are for knowing the present. Your servant asks to borrow the near as illustration: in the Zhenguan era, the Wan Nian district assistant Sima Xuanjing twisted the law and adorned cleverness to seek illicit gain; Taizong abandoned him in the market.
translations.idiomatic: Bright mirrors reveal forms; past events illuminate the present. Let me cite recent examples. In the Zhenguan era, Wan Nian district assistant Sima Xuanjing twisted the law for illicit gain; Taizong had him executed in the marketplace.

sentences.zh: 後征高麗，總管張君乂不進擊賊，斬之旗下。

translations.literal: Later, in the campaign against Goguryeo, the commander-in-chief Zhang Junyi did not advance to strike the bandits and was beheaded beneath his banner.
translations.idiomatic: Later, campaigning against Goguryeo, commander Zhang Junyi failed to advance against the enemy and was beheaded beneath his standard.

sentences.zh: 臣以為偽勛之罪，多於玄景；

translations.literal: Your servant holds that the crime of false merit is greater than that of Xuanjing.
translations.idiomatic: The crime of falsifying merit records exceeds Xuanjing's offense.

sentences.zh: 仁貴等敗，重於君乂。

translations.literal: The defeat of Rengui and the others is heavier than that of Junyi.
translations.idiomatic: The defeats of Rengui and his fellows weigh more heavily than Junyi's failure.

sentences.zh: 使早誅之，則諸將豈復有負哉？

translations.literal: Had they been punished early, would the various generals again have been remiss?
translations.idiomatic: Had they been punished promptly, would other generals still have failed in their duty?

sentences.zh: 慈父多敗子，嚴家無格虜。

translations.literal: A fond father has many failed sons; a strict household has no unruly captives.
translations.idiomatic: An indulgent father breeds failed sons; a strict household has no unruly servants.

sentences.zh: 且人主病不廣大，人臣病不節儉，臣恐陛下病之於不廣大，過在於慈父，斯日月一蝕也。

translations.literal: Moreover, the sovereign's ailment is lack of breadth; the minister's ailment is lack of thrift. Your servant fears Your Majesty's ailment lies in lack of breadth, the fault of the fond father—this is like the sun and moon suffering an eclipse.
translations.idiomatic: The sovereign's fault is narrowness; the minister's fault is extravagance. I fear Your Majesty errs on the side of narrowness, like an indulgent father—and this, like an eclipse of sun or moon, dims the throne.

sentences.zh: 又今將吏貪暴，所務口馬、財利，臣恐戎狄之平，未可旦夕望也。

translations.literal: Moreover, today's officers and clerks are greedy and violent; what they pursue is livestock, horses, and profit. Your servant fears that pacifying the barbarians cannot be hoped for within a morning and evening.
translations.idiomatic: Today's officers are greedy and brutal, caring only for livestock, horses, and profit. I fear pacifying the frontier cannot be achieved overnight.

sentences.zh: 凡人識不經遠，皆言吐蕃戰，前隊盡，後隊方進，甲堅騎多，而山有氛瘴，官軍遠入，前無所獲，不積谷數百萬，無大舉之資。

translations.literal: Ordinary men's knowledge does not reach far; all say that in fighting Tibet the front ranks are exhausted before the rear ranks advance, armor is hard and cavalry numerous, and the mountains have miasma. Government troops entering from afar gain nothing ahead; without amassing millions in grain, there is no capital for a great campaign.
translations.idiomatic: Short-sighted men say Tibetans fight with the front ranks dying before the rear advance, that their armor is strong and cavalry numerous, and that mountain miasma blocks invasion. They claim distant campaigns gain nothing without millions of bushels of grain amassed in advance.

sentences.zh: 臣以為吐蕃之望中國，猶孤星之對太陽，有自然之大小、不疑之明暗，夷狄雖禽獸，亦知愛其性命，豈肯前盡死而後進哉！

translations.literal: Your servant holds that Tibet looking upon China is like a lone star facing the sun—there is a natural great and small, an unquestioned bright and dim. Though the barbarians are like birds and beasts, they also know to love their lives—how would they be willing to have the front ranks all die before the rear advance!
translations.idiomatic: Tibet facing China is like a lone star before the sun—great and small, bright and dim, are not in doubt. Barbarians, though called beasts, still love their lives. Why would they send the front ranks to die to the last man before the rear advance?

sentences.zh: 由殘迫其人，非下所願也。

translations.literal: It is because cruelty compels their men—not what those below wish.
translations.idiomatic: They are driven by harsh compulsion from above, not by the soldiers' own will.

sentences.zh: 必其戰不顧死，則兵法許敵能鬥，當以智算取之，何憂不克哉！

translations.literal: If they indeed fight heedless of death, then military law allows that a foe who can fight should be taken by stratagem—why worry that one cannot overcome them!
translations.idiomatic: If they fight heedless of death, the art of war teaches that a resolute foe is best overcome by stratagem. Why fear that they cannot be beaten?

sentences.zh: 向使將能殺敵，橫屍蔽野，斂其頭顱以為京觀，則此虜聞官軍鐘鼓，望塵卻走，何暇前隊皆死哉！

translations.literal: If formerly generals could kill the enemy, corpses lying across the field blocking the wilds, gathering their heads to make a victory mound—then these barbarians, hearing the bells and drums of the government army, would flee at the sight of dust. How would they have leisure for the front ranks all to die!
translations.idiomatic: If our generals could slay the enemy until corpses covered the field and pile their heads in victory mounds, these barbarians would flee at the sound of our drums. Why would the front ranks need to die to the last man?

sentences.zh: 自仁貴等覆師喪氣，故虜得跳梁山谷。

translations.literal: Since Rengui and the others overturned the army and lost spirit, therefore the barbarians have been able to leap about in the valleys.
translations.idiomatic: Since Rengui's defeat broke our army's spirit, the barbarians have been free to rampage through the valleys.

sentences.zh: 又師行必藉馬力，不數十萬，不足與虜爭。

translations.literal: Moreover, when the army marches it must rely on horse power; without several hundred thousand, it is insufficient to contend with the barbarians.
translations.idiomatic: Campaigns depend on horse power; without several hundred thousand mounts, we cannot contend with the foe.

sentences.zh: 臣請天下自王公及齊人掛籍之口，人稅百錢；

translations.literal: Your servant asks that throughout All-under-Heaven, from kings and dukes down to commoners on the household registers, each person be taxed a hundred cash.
translations.idiomatic: I propose a levy of a hundred cash per registered person, from princes and dukes down to commoners.

sentences.zh: 又弛天下馬禁，使民得乘大馬，不為數限，官籍其凡，勿使得隱。

translations.literal: Also relax the empire-wide prohibition on horses, so the people may ride large horses without numerical limit; let the government register the total and not allow concealment.
translations.idiomatic: Lift the empire-wide ban on private horses so people may keep large horses without limit, with the government registering the total and forbidding concealment.

sentences.zh: 不三年，人間畜馬可五十萬，即詔州縣以所稅口錢市之，若王師大舉，一朝可用。

translations.literal: Within three years, horses raised among the people could reach five hundred thousand; then order the prefectures and districts to purchase them with the per-capita tax money. If the royal army launches a great campaign, they may be used in a single morning.
translations.idiomatic: Within three years the people could raise five hundred thousand horses. Order the prefectures to buy them with the head tax. When the royal army marches in force, they will be ready at once.

sentences.zh: 且虜以騎為強，若一切使人乘之，則市取其良，以益中國，使得漸耗虜兵之盛，國家之利也。

translations.literal: Moreover, the barbarians take cavalry as their strength; if all are made to ride horses, then purchase their fine ones to augment the central state, enabling gradual depletion of the barbarians' military strength—this is profit to the state.
translations.idiomatic: The barbarians rely on cavalry. If our people all keep horses, we can buy the best mounts for the state and gradually drain the enemy's strength—a clear gain for the realm.

sentences.zh: 高宗善之，授秘書省正字，直中書省，仗內供奉。

translations.literal: Emperor Gaozong approved it and appointed him Rectifier in the Secretariat, on duty in the Secretariat, attendant within the halberd guard.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Gaozong approved the memorial and appointed Yuanzhong Rectifier in the Secretariat, with duty at the Secretariat and attendance within the imperial guard.

sentences.zh: 遷監察御史。

translations.literal: He was transferred to investigating censor.
translations.idiomatic: He was promoted to investigating censor.

sentences.zh: 帝嘗從容曰：「外以朕為何如主？」

translations.literal: The emperor once said at ease: "Outside, what kind of ruler do they take Us to be?
translations.idiomatic: The emperor once asked casually, "How do people outside the palace regard me as a ruler?

sentences.zh: 對曰：「周成、康，漢文、景也。」

translations.literal: He replied: "Like Cheng and Kang of Zhou, Wen and Jing of Han."
translations.idiomatic: He answered, "Like King Cheng and Kang of Zhou, like Emperors Wen and Jing of Han."

sentences.zh: 「然則有遺恨乎？」

translations.literal: Then is there regret left?"
translations.idiomatic: Then is there anything you regret?"

sentences.zh: 曰：「有之。

translations.literal: He said: "There is.
translations.idiomatic: He said, "There is.

sentences.zh: 王義方一世豪英，而死草萊。

translations.literal: Wang Yifang was a hero of an age, yet died in the weeds.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Yifang was a hero of his age, yet died obscure in the fields.

sentences.zh: 議者謂陛下不能用賢。」

translations.literal: Discussants say Your Majesty cannot employ the worthy."
translations.idiomatic: Critics say Your Majesty does not employ worthy men."

sentences.zh: 帝曰：「我適用之，聞其死，顧已無及。」

translations.literal: The emperor said: "I had just employed him; when I heard of his death, looking back it was already too late."
translations.idiomatic: The emperor said, "I had just appointed him. When I heard of his death, it was already too late."

sentences.zh: 元忠曰：「劉藏器行副於才，陛下所知，今七十為尚書郎。

translations.literal: Yuanzhong said: "Liu Cangqi's conduct does not match his talent—Your Majesty knows this. Now at seventy he is a bureau director in the Secretariat.
translations.idiomatic: Yuanzhong said, "Liu Cangqi's conduct falls short of his talent, as Your Majesty knows. He is seventy and still only a bureau director in the Secretariat.

sentences.zh: 徒嘆彼而又棄此。」

translations.literal: In vain you sigh for that one yet abandon this one."
translations.idiomatic: You lament one man yet abandon another still living."

sentences.zh: 帝默然慚。

translations.literal: The emperor was silent in shame.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor fell silent, ashamed.

sentences.zh: 遷殿中侍御史。

translations.literal: He was transferred to palace attendant censor.
translations.idiomatic: He was promoted to palace attendant censor.

sentences.zh: 徐敬業舉兵，詔元忠監李孝逸軍。

translations.literal: When Xu Jingye raised troops, an edict ordered Yuanzhong to supervise Li Xiaoyi's army.
translations.idiomatic: When Xu Jingye rebelled, the court ordered Yuanzhong to supervise Li Xiaoyi's army.

sentences.zh: 至臨淮，而偏將雷仁智為賊敗，孝逸懼其鋒，按兵未敢前。

translations.literal: When they reached Linhuai, the subordinate general Lei Renzhi was defeated by the rebels. Xiaoyi feared their edge and held the army, not daring to advance.
translations.idiomatic: At Linhuai, subordinate general Lei Renzhi was defeated by the rebels. Xiaoyi feared their momentum and held his army back, daring not advance.

sentences.zh: 元忠曰：「公以宗室將，天下安危系焉。

translations.literal: Yuanzhong said: "Sir, as a general of the imperial clan, the safety and peril of All-under-Heaven are tied to you.
translations.idiomatic: Yuanzhong said, "Sir, as a commander of the imperial clan, the realm's safety rests on you.

sentences.zh: 海內承平久，聞狂狡竊發，皆傾耳翹心以待其誅。

translations.literal: Within the seas peace has long endured; hearing that a mad traitor has stolen forth in rebellion, all incline their ears and raise their hearts awaiting his execution.
translations.idiomatic: The realm has long been at peace. When word came that a mad rebel had risen, all the people strained to hear news of his destruction.

sentences.zh: 今軍不進，使遠近解情，萬有一朝廷以他將代公，且何辭？」

translations.literal: Now the army does not advance, causing near and far to lose heart. If by any chance the court replaces you with another general, what words will you have?
translations.idiomatic: If the army does not advance now, you will dishearten the realm. If the court replaces you with another commander, what excuse will you offer?

sentences.zh: 孝逸然之，乃部分進討。

translations.literal: Xiaoyi approved this and then divided the forces to advance and attack.
translations.idiomatic: Xiaoyi agreed and ordered his forces forward to attack.

sentences.zh: 時敬業保下阿谿，弟敬猷屯淮陰，鹹請「先擊下阿，下阿敗，淮陰自破。

translations.literal: At that time Jingye held Xia'a Creek; his younger brother Jingyou was stationed at Huaiyin. All requested: "First strike Xia'a; when Xia'a falls, Huaiyin will collapse of itself.
translations.idiomatic: Jingye held Xia'a Creek while his brother Jingyou camped at Huaiyin. All the officers urged, "Strike Xia'a first. Once Xia'a falls, Huaiyin will collapse on its own.

sentences.zh: 今淮陰急，敬業必救，是敵在腹背也。」

translations.literal: Now Huaiyin is urgent; Jingye is sure to rescue—then the foe will be before and behind us."
translations.idiomatic: But if we press Huaiyin now, Jingye will surely come to its relief, and the enemy will be at our front and rear.

sentences.zh: 元忠曰：「不然。

translations.literal: Yuanzhong said: "Not so.
translations.idiomatic: Yuanzhong replied, "That is not so.

sentences.zh: 賊勁兵盡守下阿，利在一決，茍有負，則大事去矣。

translations.literal: The rebels' elite troops all guard Xia'a; the advantage lies in a single decisive battle. If there is any setback, the great enterprise will be lost.
translations.idiomatic: The enemy's best troops are all holding Xia'a. Everything hangs on one decisive battle—a single defeat would ruin the entire campaign.

sentences.zh: 敬酋博徒不知戰，且其兵寡易搖，大軍臨之，勢宜克。

translations.literal: Jingyou is a gambler who knows nothing of warfare; moreover his troops are few and easily shaken. When the great army comes upon them, the situation should allow victory.
translations.idiomatic: Jingyou is a gambler who knows nothing of war. His force is small and easily unsettled; when our main army reaches him, victory should be assured.

sentences.zh: 敬業畏直搗江都，必將邀我中路，吾今乘勝進，又以逸擊勞，破之必矣。

translations.literal: Jingye fears a direct thrust at Jiangdu; he is sure to intercept us on the road. We now advance on the momentum of victory, and with rested troops strike weary ones—we are sure to break him.
translations.idiomatic: Jingye dreads a straight drive on Jiangdu and will surely try to cut us off en route. If we advance now while we still have momentum, and fresh troops hit an exhausted foe, we shall certainly defeat him.

sentences.zh: 譬之逐獸，弱者先禽。

translations.literal: It is like hunting game—the weak are taken first.
translations.idiomatic: It is like hunting wild game: you take the weak one first.

sentences.zh: 今舍必禽之弱，而趨難敵之強，非計也。」

translations.literal: Now to abandon what can surely be taken—the weak—and rush toward what is hard to match—the strong—is no plan.
translations.idiomatic: To abandon prey we could surely seize and rush at a stronger foe we can barely match would be poor strategy.

sentences.zh: 孝逸乃引兵擊淮陰，敬猷脫身遁，遂進擊敬業，平之。

translations.literal: Xiaoyi then led troops to attack Huaiyin; Jingyou escaped by body, then pressed on to attack Jingye and pacified him.
translations.idiomatic: Xiaoyi then marched against Huaiyin. Jingyou fled for his life; Xiaoyi pressed on, defeated Jingye, and put down the rebellion.

sentences.zh: 還。

translations.literal: Returned.
translations.idiomatic: He returned.

sentences.zh: 授司刑正。

translations.literal: Was appointed Director of the Bureau of Punishments.
translations.idiomatic: He was appointed Director of the Bureau of Punishments.

sentences.zh: 遷洛陽令。

translations.literal: Was transferred to Magistrate of Luoyang.
translations.idiomatic: He was promoted to Magistrate of Luoyang.

sentences.zh: 陷周興獄當死，以平揚、楚功，得流。

translations.literal: Fell into Zhou Xing's prison and was condemned to death; on account of merit in pacifying Yang and Chu, he was sentenced to exile instead.
translations.idiomatic: Implicated in Zhou Xing's investigation, he faced execution; for his role in suppressing the Yang and Chu rebellions, his sentence was reduced to exile.

sentences.zh: 歲餘，為御史中丞，復為來俊臣所構。

translations.literal: After more than a year, became Censor-in-Chief, and again was framed by Lai Junchen.
translations.idiomatic: A year later he was made Censor-in-Chief, only to be framed again by Lai Junchen.

sentences.zh: 將就刑，神色不動，前死者宗室子三十餘，屍相枕藉於前，元忠顧曰：「大丈夫行居此矣。」

translations.literal: About to undergo execution, his expression did not change. Those executed before—over thirty sons of the imperial clan—corpses piled one upon another before him. Yuanzhong looked back and said: "A great man's conduct stops here.
translations.idiomatic: As he was led to execution his face never changed. More than thirty princes of the blood had already been killed before him; corpses lay piled in heaps. Yuanzhong glanced back and said, "So this is where a true man's road ends.

sentences.zh: 俄敕鳳閣舍人王隱客馳騎免死，傳聲及於市，諸囚歡叫，元忠獨堅坐，左右命起，元忠曰：「未知實否。」

translations.literal: Soon an edict ordered Fengge Attendant Wang Yinke to gallop on horseback to remit the death sentence; the news reached even the marketplace. All the prisoners shouted with joy; Yuanzhong alone sat firm. Those beside him ordered him to rise; Yuanzhong said: "I do not know whether it is true.
translations.idiomatic: Soon an edict sent Fengge Attendant Wang Yinke riding at full speed to spare his life. Word spread even to the marketplace. The prisoners all cried out in joy, but Yuanzhong alone remained seated. His attendants told him to rise; he said, "I do not yet know if this is true.

sentences.zh: 既而隱客至，宣詔已，乃徐謝，亦不改容。

translations.literal: When Yinke arrived and the edict had been proclaimed, he then slowly bowed in thanks, yet did not change his expression.
translations.idiomatic: When Yinke arrived and read the edict, Yuanzhong rose slowly to give thanks, his face still unchanged.

sentences.zh: 流費州。

translations.literal: Was exiled to Feizhou.
translations.idiomatic: He was exiled to Feizhou.

sentences.zh: 復為中丞。

translations.literal: Again made Censor-in-Chief.
translations.idiomatic: He was again appointed Censor-in-Chief.

sentences.zh: 歲餘，陷侯思止獄，仍放嶺南。

translations.literal: After more than a year, fell into Hou Sizhi's prison, and was still sent to Lingnan.
translations.idiomatic: After another year he was caught in Hou Sizhi's investigation and banished to Lingnan.

sentences.zh: 酷吏誅，人多訟元忠者，乃召復舊官。

translations.literal: When the cruel officials were executed, many people pleaded Yuanzhong's case; he was then summoned to restore his old office.
translations.idiomatic: After the cruel officials were executed, many petitioned on Yuanzhong's behalf; he was recalled to his former rank.

sentences.zh: 因侍宴，武後曰：「卿累負謗鑠，何邪？」

translations.literal: At a banquet in attendance, Empress Wu said: "Sir, you have repeatedly borne slander that melts metal—why?
translations.idiomatic: While attending a banquet, Empress Wu said, "You have again and again been destroyed by slander—why is that?

sentences.zh: 對曰：「臣猶鹿也，羅織之吏如獵者，茍須臣肉為之羹耳，彼將殺臣以求進，臣顧何辜？」

translations.literal: He replied: "Your servant is like a deer; officials who weave false charges are like hunters. If my flesh is needed for their broth, they will kill me to seek advancement—what fault of mine is there?"
translations.idiomatic: He replied, "Your servant is like a deer, and the officers who fabricate charges are like hunters. If they need my flesh for their stew, they will kill me to get ahead—what crime have I committed?"

sentences.zh: 聖歷二年，為鳳閣侍郎、同鳳閣鸞臺平章事，俄檢校并州長史、天兵軍大總管，以備突厥。

translations.literal: In the second year of Shenglu, became Vice Minister of the Phoenix Pavilion and Associate Director of the Phoenix and Phoenix Terrace Chancellery; soon Acting Governor of Bingzhou and Grand Commander of the Tianbing Army, to guard against the Turks.
translations.idiomatic: In the second year of Shenglu (699), he was made Vice Minister of the Phoenix Pavilion and Participating Secretary of State; soon after he served as acting Governor of Bingzhou and Grand Commander of the Tianbing Army to guard against the Turks.

sentences.zh: 遷左肅政臺御史大夫，兼檢校洛州長史，治號威明。

translations.literal: Was transferred to Censor-in-Chief of the Left Suozheng Office, concurrently Acting Governor of Luozhou; his governance was famed as awe-inspiring and clear.
translations.idiomatic: He became Censor-in-Chief of the Left Suozheng Office and acting Governor of Luozhou; his administration was renowned for its stern clarity.

sentences.zh: 張易之家奴暴百姓，橫甚，元忠笞殺之，權豪憚服。

translations.literal: Zhang Yizhi's household slaves tyrannized the common people, extremely overbearing; Yuanzhong had them flogged to death, and the powerful and rich feared and submitted.
translations.idiomatic: When Zhang Yizhi's household slaves brutalized the people, Yuanzhong had them flogged to death; the powerful families were awed into submission.

sentences.zh: 俄為隴右諸軍大使，以討吐蕃；

translations.literal: Soon became Commissioner over the armies of Longyou, to campaign against the Tibetans;
translations.idiomatic: Soon he was made Commissioner over the Longyou armies to campaign against Tibet;

sentences.zh: 又為靈武道行軍大總管禦突厥。

translations.literal: Also Grand Commander on campaign of the Lingwu Circuit to repel the Turks.
translations.idiomatic: He also served as Grand Commander on the Lingwu Circuit campaign to repel the Turks.

sentences.zh: 元忠馭軍持重，雖無赫然功，而亦未嘗敗。

translations.literal: Yuanzhong managed the army with steadiness; though he had no brilliant exploits, he also never suffered defeat.
translations.idiomatic: Yuanzhong commanded with caution. He won no spectacular victories, but he never lost a battle either.

sentences.zh: 中宗在東宮，為檢校左庶子。

translations.literal: When Zhongzong was in the Eastern Palace, was Acting Left Assistant to the Heir Apparent.
translations.idiomatic: While Zhongzong was heir apparent, Yuanzhong served as Acting Left Assistant to the Crown Prince.

sentences.zh: 時二張勢傾朝廷，元忠嘗奏曰：「臣承先帝之顧，且受陛下厚恩，不能徇忠，使小人在君側，臣之罪也。」

translations.literal: At that time the Two Zhangs' power tilted the court; Yuanzhong once memorialized: "Your servant received the late emperor's care and moreover enjoys Your Majesty's great grace; unable to follow loyalty through, allowing petty men at the ruler's side—this is your servant's crime.
translations.idiomatic: The Two Zhangs then dominated the court. Yuanzhong once memorialized, "I received the late emperor's favor and Your Majesty's generous trust. My failure to be fully loyal and keep petty men from the emperor's side is my own fault.

sentences.zh: 易之等恨怒，因武後不豫，即共譖元忠與司禮丞高戩謀挾太子為耐久朋，遂下制獄。

translations.literal: Yizhi and the rest hated and raged; taking advantage of Empress Wu's illness, they jointly slandered Yuanzhong and Director of Ceremonies Gao Jian for plotting to use the Crown Prince to form a lasting friendship alliance, and had them sent to the controlled prison.
translations.idiomatic: Yizhi and his allies burned with hatred. When Empress Wu fell ill, they jointly accused Yuanzhong and Director of Ceremonies Gao Jian of plotting with the Crown Prince to form a "lasting friendship" political alliance, and had them thrown into prison.

sentences.zh: 詔皇太子、相王及宰相引元忠等辨於廷，不能決。

translations.literal: An edict ordered the Crown Prince, the Prince of Xiang, and the chief ministers to bring Yuanzhong and the others to argue the case at court; they could not decide.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor ordered the Crown Prince, the Prince of Xiang, and the chief ministers to hear Yuanzhong's defense in open court, but no verdict could be reached.

sentences.zh: 昌宗乃引張說為證，說初偽許之，至是迫使言狀，不應，後又促之，說曰：「臣不聞也。」

translations.literal: Changzong then brought Zhang Yue as witness; Yue at first falsely promised, but when forced to speak the facts, he did not respond; pressed again later, Yue said: "Your servant did not hear it.
translations.idiomatic: Changzong then summoned Zhang Yue as a witness. Yue had first agreed to testify falsely, but when pressed to describe the plot he refused. Prompted again, he said, "I heard nothing of the kind.

sentences.zh: 易之等遽曰：「說與同逆。

translations.literal: Yizhi and the rest immediately said: "Yue is of one rebellion with them.
translations.idiomatic: Yizhi and the others instantly cried, "Yue is party to the same treason!

sentences.zh: 說曩嘗謂元忠為伊、周。

translations.literal: Yue once said of Yuanzhong that he was Yi and Zhou.
translations.idiomatic: Yue had once called Yuanzhong "Yi and Zhou."

sentences.zh: 夫伊尹放太甲，周公攝王位。

translations.literal: For Yi Yin deposed Taijia; the Duke of Zhou held the royal throne in regency.
translations.idiomatic: Yi Yin banished Tai Jia; the Duke of Zhou ruled as regent.

sentences.zh: 此反狀明甚。」

translations.literal: This evidence of rebellion is exceedingly clear.
translations.idiomatic: That is open proof of rebellion!

sentences.zh: 說曰：「易之、昌宗安知伊、周，臣乃能知之。

translations.literal: Yue said: "How would Yizhi and Changzong know Yi and Zhou? Your servant is the one who can know them.
translations.idiomatic: Yue replied, "How would Yizhi and Changzong know Yi Yin and the Duke of Zhou? I am the one who knows them.

sentences.zh: 伊尹、周公，歷古以為忠臣，陛下不遣學伊、周，將何效焉？」

translations.literal: Yi Yin and the Duke of Zhou have through the ages been regarded as loyal ministers. If Your Majesty does not send us to study Yi and Zhou, whom shall we take as models?
translations.idiomatic: Yi Yin and the Duke of Zhou have always been honored as loyal ministers. If Your Majesty will not have us follow their example, whom should we imitate?

sentences.zh: 說又曰：「臣知附易之朝夕可宰相，從元忠則族滅。

translations.literal: Yue also said: "Your servant knows that cleaving to Yizhi one could be chancellor any day; following Yuanzhong means clan extermination.
translations.idiomatic: Yue added, "I know that siding with Yizhi could make one chancellor overnight, while siding with Yuanzhong means the destruction of one's entire clan.

sentences.zh: 今不敢面欺，懼元忠之冤。」

translations.literal: Now I dare not deceive Your Majesty to his face; I fear Yuanzhong's injustice.
translations.idiomatic: Today I dare not lie to Your Majesty's face for fear of wronging Yuanzhong.

sentences.zh: 後寤其讒，然重違易之，故貶元忠高要尉。

translations.literal: The Empress later awakened to their slander, yet heavily reluctant to cross Yizhi, therefore demoted Yuanzhong to Commandant of Gaoyao.
translations.idiomatic: Empress Wu eventually saw through the slander, but unwilling to defy Yizhi, she demoted Yuanzhong to Commandant of Gaoyao.

sentences.zh: 中宗復位，召為衛尉卿、同中書門下三品。

translations.literal: When Zhongzong was restored to the throne, he was summoned as Commandant of the Guard and Third Rank at the Central Secretariat and Chancellery.
translations.idiomatic: When Zhongzong was restored, Yuanzhong was recalled as Commandant of the Guard and Third-Rank Counselor of State.

sentences.zh: 不閱旬，遷兵部尚書，進侍中。

translations.literal: Within less than ten days, was transferred to Minister of War and advanced to Palace Attendant.
translations.idiomatic: Within ten days he was promoted to Minister of War and then to Palace Attendant.

sentences.zh: 武後崩，帝居喪，軍國事委元忠裁可，拜中書令，封齊國公。

translations.literal: When Empress Wu died, the Emperor was in mourning; military and state affairs were entrusted to Yuanzhong for decision; he was appointed Director of the Central Secretariat and enfeoffed as Duke of Qi.
translations.idiomatic: After Empress Wu died, the emperor went into mourning and entrusted all state and military affairs to Yuanzhong; he was made Director of the Central Secretariat and enfeoffed as Duke of Qi.

sentences.zh: 神龍二年，為尚書右僕射，知兵部尚書，當朝用事，群臣莫敢望。

translations.literal: In the second year of Shenlong, became Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, supervising the Ministry of War; he wielded power in the court, and no minister dared compare.
translations.idiomatic: In the second year of Shenlong (706), he became Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs and acting Minister of War; he dominated the court and no minister could rival him.

sentences.zh: 謁告上冢，詔宰相諸司長官祖道上東門，賜錦袍，給千騎四人侍，賜銀千兩。

translations.literal: Requested leave to visit ancestral graves; an edict ordered the chief ministers and heads of offices to give a farewell feast at the Upper East Gate, bestowing a brocade robe, providing four attendants from the Thousand Riders, and granting a thousand taels of silver.
translations.idiomatic: When he asked leave to tend his family's graves, the emperor ordered the chief ministers and department heads to give him a send-off at the Upper East Gate, with a brocade robe, four Thousand-Rider guards, and a thousand taels of silver.

sentences.zh: 元忠到家，於親戚無所賑施。

translations.literal: Yuanzhong reached home and gave no relief to relatives.
translations.idiomatic: When Yuanzhong reached home, he gave no aid to his relatives.

sentences.zh: 及還，帝為幸白馬寺迎勞之。

translations.literal: When he returned, the Emperor personally went to White Horse Temple to welcome and console him.
translations.idiomatic: On his return the emperor went in person to White Horse Temple to welcome and honor him.

sentences.zh: 安樂公主私請廢太子，求為皇太女，帝以問元忠，元忠曰：「公主而為皇太女，駙馬都尉當何名？」

translations.literal: Princess Anle privately requested to depose the Crown Prince and sought to become Imperial Heiress; the Emperor asked Yuanzhong; Yuanzhong said: "If a princess were Imperial Heiress, what title should the consort hold?
translations.idiomatic: Princess Anle privately asked to replace the Crown Prince and be named Imperial Heiress. When the emperor consulted Yuanzhong, he said, "If a princess were made imperial heir, what would we call her consort?

sentences.zh: 主恚曰：「山東木強安知禮？

translations.literal: The Princess angrily said: "You stubborn blunderer from east of the mountains—how would you know propriety?
translations.idiomatic: The princess flared up: "You stiff-necked fool from east of the mountains—what do you know of ritual?

sentences.zh: 阿母子尚為天子，我何嫌？」

translations.literal: Even A-mu became Son of Heaven—what would I scruple at?
translations.idiomatic: "A-mu" became emperor—why should I hold back?

sentences.zh: 宮中謂武後為阿母子，故主稱之。

translations.literal: The palace called Empress Wu "A-mu mother-son"; hence the Princess called her so.
translations.idiomatic: The court called Empress Wu "A-mu"; that is why the princess used the name.

sentences.zh: 元忠固稱不可，自是語塞。

translations.literal: Yuanzhong firmly declared it impossible; from then on speech was stopped.
translations.idiomatic: Yuanzhong firmly refused, and from then on she could not get her way.

sentences.zh: 武三思用事，京兆韋月將、渤海高軫上書言其惡，帝搒殺之，後莫敢言。

translations.literal: Wu Sansi wielded power; Wei Yuejiang of Jingzhao and Gao Zhen of Bohai submitted memorials speaking of his evil; the Emperor had them beaten to death; afterward none dared speak.
translations.idiomatic: When Wu Sansi dominated the government, Wei Yuejiang of Jingzhao and Gao Zhen of Bohai memorialized against him; the emperor had them beaten to death, and afterward no one dared speak out.

sentences.zh: 王同皎謀誅三思，不克，反被族。

translations.literal: Wang Tongjiao plotted to execute Sansi; it did not succeed, and he in turn was clan-exterminated.
translations.idiomatic: Wang Tongjiao plotted to kill Sansi but failed and was executed along with his entire clan.

sentences.zh: 元忠居其間，依違無所建明。

translations.literal: Yuanzhong dwelt between these events, wavering with nothing to establish or clarify.
translations.idiomatic: Yuanzhong stood by throughout, wavering and offering no clear counsel.

sentences.zh: 初，元忠相武後，有清正名，至是輔政，天下傾望，冀幹正王室，而稍憚權幸，不能賞善罰惡，譽望大減。

translations.literal: Initially, when Yuanzhong served as chancellor under Empress Wu, he had a reputation for integrity; now assisting in government, all under Heaven leaned their hopes on him, expecting him to set the royal house straight; yet he slightly feared the powerful favorites, unable to reward good and punish evil—his renown greatly diminished.
translations.idiomatic: Yuanzhong had once served Empress Wu with a reputation for upright integrity. Now that he was in power the whole realm looked to him to set the dynasty right, but he grew fearful of the favored few and neither rewarded virtue nor punished vice; his standing fell sharply.

sentences.zh: 陳郡男子袁楚客者以書規之曰：

translations.literal: A man of Chen commandery, Yuan Chuke, admonished him in a letter, saying:
translations.idiomatic: Yuan Chuke, a commoner from Chen commandery, wrote to admonish him:

sentences.zh: 今皇帝新服厥德，任官惟賢才，左右惟其人，因以布大化，充古誼，以正天下。

translations.literal: Now the Emperor has newly taken upon himself his virtue, appointing officials only for talent, keeping at his side only the right men—thereby to spread great transformation, fulfill ancient righteousness, and set All-under-Heaven right.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor has newly assumed his virtuous rule, appointing talent alone to office and keeping worthy men at his side, so that he may spread great reform, fulfill the ideals of antiquity, and set the realm right.

sentences.zh: 君侯安得事循默哉？

translations.literal: How can you, my lord, follow silence in your affairs?
translations.idiomatic: How can you, my lord, remain silent on these matters?

sentences.zh: 茍利社稷，專之可也。

translations.literal: If it benefits the altars of soil and grain, you may act on your own authority.
translations.idiomatic: If the state would benefit, you may act on your own authority.

sentences.zh: 夫安天下者先正其本，本正則天下固，國之興亡系焉。

translations.literal: He who would settle All-under-Heaven first sets straight the root; when the root is straight the realm is firm—on this the rise and fall of the state depend.
translations.idiomatic: To secure the realm one must first set the foundation right; when the foundation is sound the realm is stable, and upon this the fate of the state depends.

sentences.zh: 太子天下本，譬之大樹，無本則枝葉零悴，國無太子，朝野不安。

translations.literal: The Crown Prince is the root of All-under-Heaven, like a great tree—without root the branches and leaves wither; a state without a Crown Prince, court and countryside are unsettled.
translations.idiomatic: The Crown Prince is the root of the realm, like a great tree: without roots the branches wither; without an heir the court and countryside cannot rest easy.

sentences.zh: 儲君有次及之勢，故師保教以君人之道，用蘊崇其德，所以重天下也。

translations.literal: The heir apparent has the momentum of succession in order; hence tutors and guardians teach him the Way of ruling men, by means accumulating and elevating his virtue—this is how All-under-Heaven is weighted.
translations.idiomatic: Because the heir stands next in line to rule, tutors and guardians teach him how to govern and nurture his virtue—that is how the realm is anchored.

sentences.zh: 今皇子既長，未定嫡嗣，是天下無本。

translations.literal: Now the princes have already grown, yet the legitimate succession is not fixed—this is All-under-Heaven without root.
translations.idiomatic: The princes are grown, yet no legitimate successor has been chosen—the realm has no foundation.

sentences.zh: 天下無本，猶樹而亡根，枝葉何以存乎？

translations.literal: All-under-Heaven without root is like a tree without roots—how can branches and leaves remain?
translations.idiomatic: If the realm has no root, it is like a tree without roots—how can the branches survive?

sentences.zh: 願君侯以清宴之間言於上，擇賢而立之，此安天下之道。

translations.literal: I wish my lord, at a moment of quiet leisure, to speak to the sovereign, choose the worthy and establish him—this is the Way to settle All-under-Heaven.
translations.idiomatic: I urge you to speak to the emperor at some quiet moment, choose a worthy heir and establish him—that is the path to peace under heaven.

sentences.zh: 曠而不置，朝廷一失也。

translations.literal: Leaving it vacant and unset—this is the court's first failure.
translations.idiomatic: Failing to appoint an heir is the court's first error.

sentences.zh: 女有內則，男有外傅，豈相濫哉？

translations.literal: Women have inner norms; men have outer tutors—how could these be confused?
translations.idiomatic: Women have domestic rules and men have external instructors—must the two be confused?

sentences.zh: 幕府者，丈夫之職。

translations.literal: A staff headquarters is a man's office.
translations.idiomatic: A princely staff is a man's domain.

sentences.zh: 今公主並開府置吏，以女處男職，所謂長陰抑陽也，而望陰陽不愆、風雨時若，得乎？

translations.literal: Now princesses all open offices and appoint officials, placing women in men's posts—what is called elevating yin and suppressing yang—yet hoping yin and yang are not out of balance and wind and rain come in season—can it be?
translations.idiomatic: Now princesses all maintain their own offices and appoint officials—women filling men's roles, what is called exalting yin and suppressing yang—and yet you expect harmony between yin and yang and timely rains?

sentences.zh: 此朝廷二失也。

translations.literal: This is the court's second failure.
translations.idiomatic: That is the court's second error.

sentences.zh: 今度人既多，緇衣半道，不本行業，專以重寶附權門，皆有定直。

translations.literal: Now ordained persons are many; black robes half fill the roads; they do not base themselves on their calling but devote heavy treasures to attach to powerful houses—all have fixed prices.
translations.idiomatic: Monks and nuns now crowd the roads, abandoning their calling to shower gifts on the powerful, each with a fixed price.

sentences.zh: 昔之賣官，錢入公府，今之賣度，錢入私家。

translations.literal: Formerly selling offices, money entered the public treasury; now selling ordination, money enters private homes.
translations.idiomatic: Once offices were sold and the money went to the treasury; now ordinations are sold and the money goes to private pockets.

sentences.zh: 以茲入道，徒為遊食。

translations.literal: With this they enter the Way, merely becoming wandering idlers.
translations.idiomatic: Men enter the clergy this way only to become idle wanderers.

sentences.zh: 此朝廷三失也。

translations.literal: This is the court's third failure.
translations.idiomatic: That is the court's third error.

sentences.zh: 唯名與器，不可以假人。

translations.literal: Names and regalia alone may not be lent to others.
translations.idiomatic: Titles and insignia must not be given away casually.

sentences.zh: 故曰：「天工，人其代之。」

translations.literal: Hence it is said: "Heaven's work—men must take its place.
translations.idiomatic: As the saying runs, "Heaven's work must be done by men.

sentences.zh: 夫代天，非材不可也。

translations.literal: To stand in Heaven's place—without talent it cannot be done.
translations.idiomatic: To stand in heaven's place, only the capable will do.

sentences.zh: 代非其人，必失天意。

translations.literal: If one who is not the right person stands in, Heaven's intent must be lost.
translations.idiomatic: Put the wrong man in that role and heaven's intent is lost.

sentences.zh: 失天意而無患禍，未之有也。

translations.literal: To lose Heaven's intent yet have no calamity or harm—never has there been such a thing.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven's displeasure without disaster—there is no such thing.

sentences.zh: 今倡優之輩，因耳目之好，遂授以官，非輕朝廷、亂正法邪？

translations.literal: Now singers and actors, by reason of delight to the ears and eyes, are straightway granted office—is this not making light of the court and disordering proper law?
translations.idiomatic: Entertainers now receive official rank because they please the ear and eye—is that not to mock the court and corrupt the law?

sentences.zh: 人君無私，私怒害物，私賞費財，況私人以官乎？

translations.literal: A ruler has no private favorites; private anger harms things, private reward wastes wealth—how much more giving office to private favorites?
translations.idiomatic: A ruler should show no favoritism; private anger destroys, private rewards waste treasure—how much worse to give offices to favorites?

sentences.zh: 此朝廷四失也。

translations.literal: This is the court's fourth failure.
translations.idiomatic: That is the court's fourth error.

sentences.zh: 賢者邦家之光，任之致治，棄之生亂。

translations.literal: The worthy are a state's glory; employing them brings order, abandoning them breeds chaos.
translations.idiomatic: The worthy are a nation's glory; appoint them and order follows, reject them and chaos ensues.

sentences.zh: 近詔博求多士，雖有好賢之名，無得賢之實。

translations.literal: Recently an edict broadly sought many scholars; though it bears the name of loving worth, it has not the reality of obtaining worth.
translations.idiomatic: A recent edict called broadly for men of talent, but though it bore the name of seeking the wise, it produced no wise men.

sentences.zh: 蓋有司選士，非賄即勢，上失天心，下違人望，非為官擇吏，乃為人擇官。

translations.literal: Probably the offices selecting scholars—either bribes or power; above they lose Heaven's heart, below they violate men's hopes—not choosing officials for posts, but choosing posts for men.
translations.idiomatic: The selection boards choose by bribery or influence, losing heaven's favor and the people's trust—not picking officials for the posts but picking posts for the men.

sentences.zh: 葛洪有言：「舉秀才，不知書；

translations.literal: Ge Hong has a saying: "Recommending xiucai—they know not books;
translations.idiomatic: Ge Hong wrote: "They recommend 'cultivated talent' who cannot read;

sentences.zh: 察孝廉，濁如泥；

translations.literal: examining xiaolian—muddy as clay;
translations.idiomatic: they examine 'filial and incorrupt' who are filthy as mud;

sentences.zh: 高第賢良吝如蛙。

translations.literal: high-ranking xianliang—stingy as frogs.
translations.idiomatic: and promote 'worthy and good' who are tight-fisted as frogs."

sentences.zh: 此朝廷五失也。

translations.literal: This is the court's fifth failure.
translations.idiomatic: That is the court's fifth error.

sentences.zh: 閹豎者，給宮掖掃除事，古以奴隸畜之。

translations.literal: Eunuchs serve palace-women's sweepings and cleaning; in antiquity they were kept like slaves.
translations.idiomatic: Eunuchs were meant to sweep the inner quarters; antiquity kept them as slaves.

sentences.zh: 中古以來，大道乖喪，疏賢哲，親近習，乃委之以事，授之以權。

translations.literal: Since the middle antiquity, the Great Way has been lost; distancing the wise and sages, drawing near familiar companions—they then entrusted them with affairs and granted them power.
translations.idiomatic: Since later ages the Way has decayed: rulers spurned the wise and favored flatterers, entrusting them with affairs and handing them power.

sentences.zh: 故豎刁亂齊，伊戾敗宋。

translations.literal: Hence Shu Diao threw Qi into chaos, Yi Li ruined Song.
translations.idiomatic: Hence Shu Diao brought chaos to Qi and Yi Li ruined Song.

sentences.zh: 君側之人，眾所畏懼，所謂鷹頭之蠅、廟垣之鼠者也。

translations.literal: Men at the ruler's side—all fear them; what are called flies on the falcon's head, rats in the temple wall.
translations.idiomatic: Men at the ruler's elbow are universally feared—the "flies on the hawk's head" and "rats in the temple wall."

sentences.zh: 後漢時用事尤甚，晚節卒亂天下。

translations.literal: In Later Han their wielding of power was especially severe; in their final years they at last threw All-under-Heaven into chaos.
translations.idiomatic: Under Later Han they grew especially powerful and in the dynasty's last years threw the realm into chaos.

sentences.zh: 今大君中興，獨有閹豎坐升班秩，既無正闕，率授員外，乃盈千人，綰青紫，耗府藏。

translations.literal: Now the Great Lord has revived the dynasty, yet eunuchs alone sit and ascend court ranks; there being no regular vacancies, as a rule they are given surplus appointments—more than a thousand thread purple and blue, draining the treasury.
translations.idiomatic: Now in this restoration eunuchs alone sit in court rank though no regular posts exist; they are routinely given supernumerary titles—more than a thousand wearing purple and scarlet, draining the treasury.

sentences.zh: 前事之驗，後事之師。

translations.literal: Former affairs are verification; later affairs take them as teachers.
translations.idiomatic: Past events are the proof; let them teach the future.

sentences.zh: 此朝廷六失也。

translations.literal: This is the court's sixth failure.
translations.idiomatic: That is the court's sixth error.

sentences.zh: 古者茅茨采椽，以儉約遺子孫，所以愛力也。

translations.literal: In antiquity, thatched roofs and plain rafters were used, passing frugality down to descendants—this was how one cherished one's strength.
translations.idiomatic: In antiquity people lived in thatched cottages with plain rafters, bequeathing thrift to their descendants as a way to conserve the state's resources.

sentences.zh: 今公主所賞傾庫府，所造皆官供，其疏築臺沼，崇峙觀廡，山無本石，木無近產，造之終歲，功用不絕。

translations.literal: Now the princess's rewards drain the treasury, and all she constructs is supplied by the government. She lays out terraces and ponds, raises lofty halls and galleries; stones have no native mountain, timber no nearby source—building goes on the whole year, labor never ceasing.
translations.idiomatic: Now princesses receive rewards that empty the treasury, and everything they build comes from public supplies. They dredge ponds and erect terraces, raise towering halls and galleries, hauling stone from distant mountains and timber from far-off forests—construction continues year-round without pause.

sentences.zh: 夫為君所以養人，非以害人，今外戚不助養而反害之，是使人主受謗天下。

translations.literal: For a ruler's purpose in governing is to nurture the people, not to harm them. Now the consort kin do not help nurture but instead harm them—this makes the sovereign suffer reproach throughout the realm.
translations.idiomatic: The purpose of rule is to nourish the people, not to injure them. Yet consort relatives now fail to help nurture them and instead do them harm, bringing slander upon the sovereign throughout the realm.

sentences.zh: 此朝廷七失也。

translations.literal: This is the court's seventh failure.
translations.idiomatic: This is the seventh failing of the court.

sentences.zh: 官以安人，非以害於人也。

translations.literal: Offices exist to settle the people, not to harm people.
translations.idiomatic: Offices exist to bring the people peace, not to do them injury.

sentences.zh: 先王欲人治必選材，欲人安必省事，此誠同天下憂也。

translations.literal: Former kings, wishing the people well governed, always selected talent; wishing the people at ease, always reduced affairs—this truly shares the realm's worry.
translations.idiomatic: When former kings sought good governance, they always chose the able; when they sought the people's peace, they always streamlined government. This is truly to share the realm's cares.

sentences.zh: 人有樂，君共之，君有樂，人慶之，可謂同樂矣。

translations.literal: When the people have joy, the ruler shares it; when the ruler has joy, the people celebrate it—this may be called shared joy.
translations.idiomatic: When the people rejoice, the ruler rejoices with them; when the ruler rejoices, the people celebrate—this is true shared joy.

sentences.zh: 如此，則上下無間，而均一體也。

translations.literal: Thus, above and below have no gap, and are one body equally.
translations.idiomatic: In this way, ruler and ruled are without division, united as one body.

sentences.zh: 今天下困窮，州牧、縣宰，非以選進，割剝自私，人不聊生，是下有憂而上不恤也。

translations.literal: Now the realm is exhausted and impoverished. Prefects and magistrates, not advanced by selection, exploit and strip for their own profit; the people cannot sustain life—below there is suffering, yet above shows no compassion.
translations.idiomatic: The realm is now exhausted. Prefects and county magistrates, appointed without proper selection, plunder for private gain while the people cannot survive—distress below, yet no concern above.

sentences.zh: 而更員外置官，非助桀歟？

translations.literal: Yet moreover surplus officials are appointed—is this not aiding Jie?
translations.idiomatic: And on top of this, surplus officials are being created—is this not playing the tyrant Jie's role?

sentences.zh: 夫人情自以員外吏，恐下不己畏也，必峻法懼之；

translations.literal: For human disposition, taking oneself as a surplus official, fearing those below do not fear oneself, one must use harsh laws to frighten them;
translations.idiomatic: Men appointed as surplus officials, fearing subordinates will not fear them, inevitably resort to harsh laws to intimidate;

sentences.zh: 恐財不己奉也，必枉道奪之。

translations.literal: fearing wealth does not suffice for oneself, must by crooked ways seize it.
translations.idiomatic: and fearing their income will not suffice, inevitably seize wealth by unjust means.

sentences.zh: 欲不亂，可得哉？

translations.literal: Wishing not to have disorder—can this be obtained?
translations.idiomatic: How can order be maintained under such conditions?

sentences.zh: 古語有之，十羊九牧，羊既不得食，人亦不得息。

translations.literal: An old saying has it: ten sheep, nine herdsmen—the sheep cannot eat, and the men also cannot rest.
translations.idiomatic: An old saying runs: ten sheep tended by nine herdsmen—the sheep go unfed and the herdsmen get no rest.

sentences.zh: 《書》曰：「官不必備，惟其人。」

translations.literal: The 《Book of Documents》 says: "Offices need not be fully staffed—only the right men matter.
translations.idiomatic: The 《Book of Documents》 states: "Offices need not be fully filled—only the right men matter.

sentences.zh: 此言正員猶難其備，況員之外乎！

translations.literal: This saying means even regular posts are hard to fill properly—how much more those beyond the quota!
translations.idiomatic: If even regular positions are hard to fill with the right men, how much more so surplus appointments!

sentences.zh: 此朝廷八失也。

translations.literal: This is the court's eighth failure.
translations.idiomatic: This is the eighth failing of the court.

sentences.zh: 政出多門，大亂之漸。

translations.literal: Policy issuing from many gates—the beginning of great disorder.
translations.idiomatic: When policy issues from many hands, great disorder is not far behind.

sentences.zh: 近封數夫人，皆先帝宮嬪。

translations.literal: Recently several Ladies were ennobled—all former palace women of the late emperor.
translations.idiomatic: Recently several Ladies were ennobled—all of them former consorts of the late emperor.

sentences.zh: 以為備內職，則不當知外；

translations.literal: If regarded as filling inner duties, they should not know of outer affairs;
translations.idiomatic: If they are to fill inner court duties, they should not know of affairs outside;

sentences.zh: 不備內職，則自可處外。

translations.literal: if not filling inner duties, they naturally may dwell outside.
translations.idiomatic: if they do not fill inner duties, they naturally may remain outside.

sentences.zh: 而令出入禁掖，使內言必出，外言必入，固將弄君之法，縱而不禁，非所以重宗廟、固國家。

translations.literal: Yet they are allowed to enter and leave the inner palace, making inner words always go out and outer words always come in—they will surely manipulate the ruler's laws, indulged without restraint. This is not the way to honor the ancestral temple and consolidate the state.
translations.idiomatic: Yet they are permitted to come and go within the forbidden inner quarters, so that inner words always leak out and outer words always filter in—they will surely twist the ruler's laws, indulged without restraint. This is no way to honor the ancestral temple and secure the state.

sentences.zh: 孔子曰：「彼婦之口，可以出走；

translations.literal: Confucius said: "That woman's mouth can make one flee;
translations.idiomatic: Confucius said: "That woman's tongue can drive a man from his home;

sentences.zh: 彼婦之謁，可以死敗。」

translations.literal: that woman's petition can bring death and ruin.
translations.idiomatic: that woman's pleading can bring death and ruin.

sentences.zh: 此朝廷九失也。

translations.literal: This is the court's ninth failure.
translations.idiomatic: This is the ninth failing of the court.

sentences.zh: 不以道事其君者，所以危天下也，危天下之臣不可不逐，安天下之臣不可不任。

translations.literal: Those who do not serve their lord by the Way are what endanger the realm. Ministers who endanger the realm must be expelled; ministers who secure the realm must be employed.
translations.idiomatic: Those who do not serve their sovereign by the Way endanger the realm. Ministers who endanger the realm must be driven out; ministers who secure the realm must be entrusted with office.

sentences.zh: 今有引鬼神、執左道以惑主者，托鬼神為難知，故致其詐，而據非才之地，食非德之祿，此國盜也。

translations.literal: Now there are those who invoke ghosts and spirits, wield heterodox ways to bewilder the sovereign, using spirits' unknowability to practice deceit, yet occupy posts for which they lack talent and consume stipends they have not earned—these are thieves of the state.
translations.idiomatic: Now there are men who invoke ghosts and spirits and wield heterodox arts to bewilder the sovereign, exploiting the unknowability of the supernatural to practice fraud, yet hold posts for which they lack talent and draw stipends they have not earned—these are thieves of the state.

sentences.zh: 《傳》曰：「國將興，聽於民，將亡，聽於神。」

translations.literal: The 《Commentary》 says: "When a state is about to rise, it heeds the people; when about to perish, it heeds the spirits.
translations.idiomatic: The 《Commentary》 says: "When a state is about to flourish, it listens to the people; when it is about to perish, it listens to the spirits.

sentences.zh: 今幾聽於神乎？

translations.literal: Are we now close to heeding spirits?
translations.idiomatic: Are we not now close to heeding spirits instead?

sentences.zh: 此朝廷十失也。

translations.literal: This is the court's tenth failure.
translations.idiomatic: This is the tenth failing of the court.

sentences.zh: 君侯不正，誰與正之？

translations.literal: If the lord is not upright, who will make him upright?
translations.idiomatic: If the sovereign is not upright, who will set him right?

sentences.zh: 元忠得書益慚。

translations.literal: Yuanzhong received the letter and grew all the more ashamed.
translations.idiomatic: When Yuanzhong received the letter, he felt all the more ashamed.

sentences.zh: 以三思專權，思有以誅之。

translations.literal: Because Sansi monopolized power, he thought how he might execute him.
translations.idiomatic: Because Wu Sansi monopolized power, Yuanzhong sought a way to have him killed.

sentences.zh: 會節湣太子起兵，與聞其謀。

translations.literal: It happened that the Jiemin Crown Prince raised troops; Yuanzhong learned of the plot.
translations.idiomatic: When the Jiemin Crown Prince raised troops, Yuanzhong learned of the conspiracy.

sentences.zh: 太子已誅三思，引兵走闕下，元忠子太仆少卿升遇於永安門，太子脅使從戰，已而被殺。

translations.literal: After the Crown Prince had killed Sansi, he led troops to the palace gate. Yuanzhong's son Sheng, Vice Minister of the Imperial Stud, encountered him at Yong'an Gate; the Crown Prince coerced him into following the fight, and afterward he was killed.
translations.idiomatic: After the Crown Prince had killed Wu Sansi, he led his troops to the palace gates. Yuanzhong's son Sheng, Vice Minister of the Imperial Stud, met him at Yong'an Gate; the Crown Prince forced him to join the battle, and afterward he was killed.

sentences.zh: 議者未辨逆順，元忠誦言曰：「既誅賊謝天下，雖死鼎鑊所甘心。

translations.literal: Those deliberating had not yet distinguished rebel from loyal. Yuanzhong spoke aloud: "Having executed the villain and answered to the realm, even death in the cauldron I would accept willingly.
translations.idiomatic: While deliberators had not yet sorted rebel from loyal, Yuanzhong declared aloud: "Having slain the traitor and answered to the realm, I would gladly accept death in the cauldron.

sentences.zh: 惟皇太子沒為恨耳。」

translations.literal: Only that the Crown Prince perished is my regret.
translations.idiomatic: My only regret is that the Crown Prince perished.

sentences.zh: 帝以其嘗有功，且為高宗、武後素所禮，置不問。

translations.literal: The Emperor, because he had once rendered service and had long been honored by Emperor Gaozong and Empress Wu, let the matter drop.
translations.idiomatic: The Emperor, because Yuanzhong had once rendered service and had long been honored by Emperor Gaozong and Empress Wu, let the matter drop.

sentences.zh: 宗楚客、紀處訥大怒，固請夷其族，不聽。

translations.literal: Zong Chuke and Ji Chune were furious and repeatedly requested his clan be exterminated; the Emperor did not agree.
translations.idiomatic: Zong Chuke and Ji Chune were furious and repeatedly demanded that his entire clan be exterminated, but the Emperor refused.

sentences.zh: 元忠不自安，上政事及國封，詔以特進、齊國公致仕，朝朔望。

translations.literal: Yuanzhong felt ill at ease and submitted his office and fief. An edict granted him Special Advancement, Duke of Qi, and retirement, with attendance at the first and fifteenth of the month.
translations.idiomatic: Feeling ill at ease, Yuanzhong submitted his office and fief. An edict granted him the title Special Advancement and Duke of Qi and allowed him to retire, with attendance at court on the first and fifteenth of each month.

sentences.zh: 楚客等引右衛郎將姚廷筠為御史中丞，暴奏反狀，繇是貶渠州司馬。

translations.literal: Chuke and others installed Right Guards General Yao Tingyun as Censor-in-Chief, who openly memorialized treasonous conduct; thereby Yuanzhong was demoted to Deputy Prefect of Quzhou.
translations.idiomatic: Chuke and his allies installed Right Guards General Yao Tingyun as Censor-in-Chief, who openly memorialized charges of treason; Yuanzhong was thereby demoted to Deputy Prefect of Quzhou.

sentences.zh: 楊再思、李嶠皆希順楚客，傅致元忠罪，唯蕭至忠議當申宥之。

translations.literal: Yang Zaisi and Li Qiao both curried favor with Chuke and piled charges on Yuanzhong; only Xiao Zhizhong argued he should be granted clemency.
translations.idiomatic: Yang Zaisi and Li Qiao both curried favor with Chuke and heaped charges on Yuanzhong; only Xiao Zhizhong argued that he should be shown clemency.

sentences.zh: 楚客復遣再思與冉祖雍奏元忠緣逆不宜處內地，監察御史袁守一固請行誅，遂貶務川尉。

translations.literal: Chuke again sent Zaisi and Ran Zuyong to memorialize that Yuanzhong, having ties to rebellion, should not remain in the interior; Supervising Censor Yuan Shouyi repeatedly requested execution; he was finally demoted to Commandant of Wuchuan.
translations.idiomatic: Chuke again sent Zaisi and Ran Zuyong to memorialize that Yuanzhong, having ties to rebellion, should not remain in the interior; Supervising Censor Yuan Shouyi repeatedly demanded execution; Yuanzhong was finally demoted to Commandant of Wuchuan.

sentences.zh: 守一又劾：「天後嘗不豫，狄仁傑請陛下監國，元忠止之，此其逆久萌。」

translations.literal: Shouyi also impeached: "When the Heavenly Empress was once unwell, Di Renjie asked Your Majesty to supervise the realm, and Yuanzhong stopped it—his rebellious intent had long been budding.
translations.idiomatic: Shouyi also impeached him, saying: "When the Heavenly Empress was once unwell, Di Renjie asked Your Majesty to supervise the realm, and Yuanzhong blocked it—his rebellious intent had long been budding.

sentences.zh: 帝謂楊再思曰：「守一非是。

translations.literal: The Emperor said to Yang Zaisi: "Shouyi is wrong.
translations.idiomatic: The Emperor said to Yang Zaisi: "Shouyi is wrong.

sentences.zh: 事君者一其心，豈有上少疾遽異論哉？

translations.literal: One who serves his lord keeps one heart—how could there be sudden divergent opinions when the ruler is briefly ill?
translations.idiomatic: One who serves his sovereign keeps a single heart—how could there be sudden divergent opinions when the ruler is briefly ill?

sentences.zh: 朕未見元忠過也。」

translations.literal: I have not seen any fault in Yuanzhong."
translations.idiomatic: I have seen no fault in Yuanzhong."

sentences.zh: 元忠至涪陵，卒，年七十餘。

translations.literal: Yuanzhong reached Fuling and died, aged over seventy.
translations.idiomatic: Yuanzhong reached Fuling and died there, aged over seventy.

sentences.zh: 景龍四年，贈尚書左僕射、齊國公、本州刺史。

translations.literal: In the fourth year of Jinglong, posthumously granted Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, Duke of Qi, and Prefect of his home province.
translations.idiomatic: In the fourth year of Jinglong, he was posthumously granted the titles Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, Duke of Qi, and Prefect of his home province.

sentences.zh: 睿宗詔陪葬定陵，以實封一百五十戶賜其子晃。

translations.literal: Emperor Ruizong ordered burial near Dingling, granting his son Huang one hundred fifty taxable households as a fief.
